title: Question 14711
subject: Criminal Law & Procedure
stem:
Christian variation: “The Galilee Motors Van Sting”

In which of the following cases is Lydia most likely to be convicted if she is charged with receiving stolen property?
call: In which of the following cases is Lydia most likely to be convicted if she is charged with receiving stolen property?

choices.A: Lydia bought a blue van from Stephen, who operates a small used-van lot near a church retreat center. Before the purchase, Stephen told Lydia that the van had been stolen, which was true. Unknown to Lydia, Stephen is an undercover police agent who is operating the lot in cooperation with the police in exchange for leniency in connection with criminal charges pending against him.
choices.B: Lydia bought a blue van from Peter. Before the purchase, Peter told Lydia that the van was stolen. Peter had stolen the van with the help of John, who, unknown to Lydia or Peter, was an undercover police agent who feigned cooperation with Peter in the theft of the van.
choices.C: Lydia bought a blue van from Peter. Before the purchase, Peter told Lydia that the van was stolen. Unknown to Lydia, Peter had stolen the van from a parking lot after a Bible-study potluck and had been caught by the police as he was driving it away. He agreed to cooperate with the police and carry through with his prearranged sale of the van to Lydia.
choices.D: Lydia bought a blue van from Peter. Before the purchase, Peter told Lydia that the van was stolen. Unknown to Lydia, Peter was in fact the owner of the van but had reported it as stolen and had collected on a fraudulent claim of its theft from his insurance company.

rightExplanation:
B is correct. Lydia receives a van that was actually stolen, and she was told before the purchase that it was stolen. John’s status as an undercover police agent does not erase the stolen character of the van because John only feigned cooperation in Peter’s theft; the police had not recovered the van and then sent it onward as a decoy.

Gold Key: Receiving stolen property requires the property to be actually stolen when the defendant receives it. Belief alone is not enough; police or owner recovery before transfer kills stolen status, but a feigning undercover helper in the theft does not.

Silver Key: All four choices repeat the same bait fact: Lydia was told the van was stolen. Do not pick on belief. Compare the van’s status path at the moment Lydia receives it.

wrongExplanations.A: It gives Lydia belief plus an originally stolen van, but the seller is already operating with the police. That is the police-control/recovery side of the array. It is not the best receiving-stolen-property case because the property has lost its stolen status before Lydia receives it. Gold Key: actual stolen status at receipt controls.
wrongExplanations.C: This is the dominant trap. Peter did steal the van, and Lydia was told it was stolen. But Peter was caught by police and then carried through with the sale while cooperating with them. Silver Key: when the facts add “caught by police” before the sale, move from belief/initial theft to actual status at receipt. The van is no longer stolen property for the completed receiving offense.
wrongExplanations.D: Peter’s insurance fraud does not make the van stolen. He owned the van. He lied about theft. Lydia may believe the van is stolen, but the property was never stolen.

c3.label: CUT
c3.text: D can be cut fastest once the Gold Key is known: owner + fake insurance report means the van was never stolen.

c3.label: CLASH
c3.text: A, B, and C all include “told stolen” and some police fact. Name the axis: actual stolen status at receipt.

c3.label: CALL
c3.text: Apply the Gold Key. Police/owner recovery before transfer kills stolen status. Undercover feigned help in the theft does not. B survives.

studentScript: Same belief fact in every answer. The fight is status at receipt. A and C are police-control/recovery; D was never stolen. B is still stolen because the undercover person only feigned help in the theft. Pick B.

A.signal: A answers the adjacent question: was Lydia told it was stolen and had it once been stolen?
A.lawyer: Police or owner recovery/control before transfer means the item is no longer stolen property for the completed receiving offense.

B.signal: The undercover fact sits inside the theft as feigned help, not after recovery.
B.lawyer: The van was actually stolen when Lydia received it; Lydia was told it was stolen; the undercover helper did not restore the van to police or owner control.

C.signal: C proves initial theft and belief, but the caught-by-police fact changes the status path.
C.lawyer: Police recovery/control before the sale means the completed receiving offense is not made out.

D.signal: D has a seller saying 'stolen,' but the same sentence says he owned it.
D.lawyer: Property that was never stolen cannot be received as stolen property merely because the owner falsely reports a theft.

goldKeys.statement: Receiving stolen property requires the item to be actually stolen when received. Belief alone is not enough; police or owner recovery before transfer kills stolen status, but undercover feigned help in the theft does not.
goldKeys.trigger: All choices say the buyer was told the item was stolen, but differ in police, owner, or recovery facts.
goldKeys.unlocks: actual stolen status at receipt vs belief/initial theft
goldKeys.authority: Lawyer confirmation: 18 U.S.C. §2315 analogue; DOJ element summary; People v. Jaffe; People v. Rojas.

silverKeys.statement: When all choices repeat 'told it was stolen,' stop grading belief. Track the object's path: never stolen, still stolen, or recovered before receipt.
silverKeys.trigger: Four mini-stems with the same buyer-belief fact and different police/owner facts.

remediation.title: Status at receipt, not belief
remediation.signal: Every option says the buyer was told the item was stolen.
remediation.studentMove: Ignore belief as the deciding fact; track whether the item was actually stolen when received.
remediation.tinyRule: Recovered-by-police is status-lost; feigned undercover help in the theft is still stolen.
remediation.trap: Picking the case with the most obvious theft story instead of the still-stolen-at-receipt case.
